a1_answer:
NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice delivers a **monitoring/indication scheme** that detects surge onset via a surge probe (specific dynamic pressure or flow coefficient sensor) and trips the compressor; your same-class departure is a **predictor based on the thermodynamic proximity of the operating point to the surge line using only existing suction/discharge pressures, motor current, and chilled-water temperature**, where the failure-physics connection is that surge is governed by the ratio of static pressure recovery to flow rate, which degrades predictably as the evaporator load (reflected in chilled-water temperature and motor current) shifts the operating point toward the left boundary of the centrifugal compressor map.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is the surge line on a typical 500 kW centrifugal chiller compressor map, which can be approximated as a static pressure recovery ratio \( R_s = P_d/P_s \) vs. flow coefficient \( \phi \). Surge occurs when the actual operating flow coefficient falls below the surge-flow coefficient for the current pressure ratio. The magnitude verification: for a 500 kW unit, typical suction pressure \( P_s \approx 4.5 \text{ bar(a)} \) and discharge \( P_d \approx 15 \text{ bar(a)} \) gives \( R_s \approx 3.33 \). Surge typically occurs at a minimum flow coefficient \( \phi_{surge} \) that is 60-70% of the design point flow. As chilled-water temperature rises (lower evaporator load), the compressor flow decreases, moving the operating point toward surge. The predictor calculates the distance to the surge line in \( \phi \)-space using the existing pressures and infers flow from motor current (since \( I \propto \text{power} \propto \text{mass flow} \times \text{pressure rise} \) for a given efficiency curve). This is a valid leading indicator because the operating point drifts over days/weeks as cooling load changes seasonally.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: an algorithm running on the existing BMS/PLC. Inputs: **ALREADY-RECORDED** suction pressure, discharge pressure, motor current, and chilled-water temperature (as stated in the problem). References: **DERIVED** surge line approximation from the compressor’s OEM data sheet (stated spec) and the relationship \( \phi \propto I / (P_d - P_s) \) (stated physics for centrifugal flow vs. power). Threshold: **DERIVED** from the 30-day warning requirement, which implies a drift rate calculation; the threshold is set at 95% of the distance to the surge line, calculated in real-time. No new sensors are installed; no surge probe is used. The algorithm continuously updates the surge proximity index \( SPI = 1 - (\phi_{op} - \phi_{surge}) / (\phi_{design} - \phi_{surge}) \).

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Same as standard practice because no hardware is added; uses existing BMS/PLC. Operability: Same, because it runs on existing software infrastructure. Maintenance: Lower than standard practice because it eliminates surge probe calibration and replacement. Rough cost class: Same (software only) or lower (no hardware). The burden is lighter, which is a benefit, not a penalty.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: 1. Retrieve 1 year of historical BMS data (suction/discharge pressure, motor current, chilled-water temperature). 2. Identify all surge trip events in that year. 3. Run the algorithm in simulation on that data to calculate the SPI at \( T-30 \) days before each trip. 4. Pass/Fail: The SPI must exceed 0.95 at \( T-30 \) days for >99% of surge events (to achieve ≤1 FA/chiller/year). 5. Duration: 1 week for historical data analysis. 6. Kill Criterion: If the algorithm fails to predict ≥95% of historical surge events at \( T-30 \) days, the method is rejected.

CONSTRAINT BIND — Primary stated indicator: **Motor current and chilled-water temperature** are the primary indicators of load drift, while **suction/discharge pressure** is the primary indicator of surge proximity. The predictor uses all four because surge is a function of both flow (inferred from current and temperature) and pressure ratio. The problem states "use only the existing suction/discharge pressure, motor current and chilled-water temperature," so these are the stated indicators. No secondary indicators are introduced.
